title: A Cell Keeps Its Answer Ready

scenes.tts: How does a cell recognize an enemy it has never met, and answer within minutes? A macrophage is a white blood cell that swallows microbes. Within minutes of touching a bacterium, it begins to change its gene expression. So what links a touch at the membrane to genes in the nucleus? The answer was waiting in the cytoplasm the whole time.
scenes.visual: A macrophage outline with a nucleus and genes; a bacterium glides in and touches the membrane while a clock sweeps; dashed question-mark boxes fill the path from the membrane to the genes; they fade and a dashed blue pair-shape appears waiting in the cytoplasm.
scenes.narration: How does a cell recognize an enemy it has never met, and answer within minutes? A macrophage is a white blood cell that swallows microbes. Within minutes of touching a bacterium, it begins to change its gene expression. So what links a touch at the membrane to genes in the nucleus? The answer was waiting in the cytoplasm the whole time.

scenes.tts: The answer is N F kappa B, a transcription factor. It is a pair of proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on. In a resting cell, it is already made and folded. It waits in the cytoplasm, held by its inhibitor, I kappa B. I kappa B covers the signal that would send N F kappa B into the nucleus.
scenes.caption: The answer is NF-κB, a transcription factor. It is a pair of proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on. In a resting cell, it is already made and folded. It waits in the cytoplasm, held by its inhibitor, IκB. IκB covers the signal that would send NF-κB into the nucleus.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the cytoplasm: NF-kB as two blue lobes with a bright tab that points at the nucleus; the red IκB cap slides over the tab and a red bar blocks the dashed path to the genes.
scenes.narration: The answer is NF-κB, a transcription factor. It is a pair of proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on. In a resting cell, it is already made and folded. It waits in the cytoplasm, held by its inhibitor, IκB. IκB covers the signal that would send NF-κB into the nucleus.

scenes.tts: A bacterial molecule, lipopolysaccharide, holds two Toll-like receptors side by side. The pair docks an adaptor, My D 88, which stacks with I R A K kinases into a tower. An activated I R A K binds TRAF 6, which builds a ubiquitin chain joined through lysine 63. Together with head-to-tail chains, it gathers TAK 1 next to I K K. TAK 1 switches on I K K, the I kappa B kinase.
scenes.caption: A bacterial molecule, lipopolysaccharide, holds two Toll-like receptors side by side. The pair docks an adaptor, MyD88, which stacks with IRAK kinases into a tower. An activated IRAK binds TRAF6, which builds a ubiquitin chain joined through lysine 63. Together with head-to-tail chains, it gathers TAK1 next to IKK. TAK1 switches on IKK, the IκB kinase.
scenes.visual: A signal runs down a relay: two receptors are pulled together by the orange molecule, a tower of three slabs forms under them, TRAF6 grows a chain of teal beads, TAK1 and IKK sit on the chain, a phosphate passes from TAK1 to IKK and IKK turns on.
scenes.narration: A bacterial molecule, lipopolysaccharide, holds two Toll-like receptors side by side. The pair docks an adaptor, MyD88, which stacks with IRAK kinases into a tower. An activated IRAK binds TRAF6, which builds a ubiquitin chain joined through lysine 63. Together with head-to-tail chains, it gathers TAK1 next to IKK. TAK1 switches on IKK, the IκB kinase.

scenes.tts: I K K adds two phosphates to I kappa B. Even then, I kappa B still holds N F kappa B. A second ligase adds a chain joined through lysine 48. That chain sends I kappa B to the proteasome, which destroys it. Now nothing covers the signal that sends N F kappa B into the nucleus.
scenes.caption: IKK adds two phosphates to IκB. Even then, IκB still holds NF-κB. A second ligase adds a chain joined through lysine 48. That chain sends IκB to the proteasome, which destroys it. Now nothing covers the signal that sends NF-κB into the nucleus.
scenes.visual: IKK sends two phosphate badges to the red IκB cap, which stays on; a ligase hangs a teal lysine-48 chain on the cap; the proteasome takes the cap and it breaks up; the bright tab on NF-kB is bare.
scenes.narration: IKK adds two phosphates to IκB. Even then, IκB still holds NF-κB. A second ligase adds a chain joined through lysine 48. That chain sends IκB to the proteasome, which destroys it. Now nothing covers the signal that sends NF-κB into the nucleus.

scenes.tts: Now N F kappa B, already folded, enters the nucleus. The two proteins wrap around the DNA, and each reads one half of its site. N F kappa B switches on its genes. Nothing had to be transcribed or translated first. So N F kappa B reaches its genes within minutes.
scenes.caption: Now NF-κB, already folded, enters the nucleus. The two proteins wrap around the DNA, and each reads one half of its site. NF-κB switches on its genes. Nothing had to be transcribed or translated first. So NF-κB reaches its genes within minutes.
scenes.visual: NF-kB drops through the nuclear envelope, which opens into a full-height nucleus; the two lobes settle on either side of a site on the DNA and the genes turn green; two ghost boxes, transcribe and translate, are crossed out; a clock sweeps.
scenes.narration: Now NF-κB, already folded, enters the nucleus. The two proteins wrap around the DNA, and each reads one half of its site. NF-κB switches on its genes. Nothing had to be transcribed or translated first. So NF-κB reaches its genes within minutes.

scenes.tts: Take a cell line with no N F kappa B activity, and block its protein synthesis. Lipopolysaccharide still makes the activity appear. So the protein must already have been there, inhibited. Here is the rule. Finish the activator, hold it outside the nucleus, and remove its inhibitor when the signal comes.

Here is the rule. Finish the activator, hold it outside the nucleus, and remove its inhibitor when the signal comes.
scenes.visual: A cell line with an empty NF-kB activity gauge and a crossed-out protein synthesis box; the orange molecule arrives and the gauge fills; the hidden NF-kB with its IκB cap appears inside the cell; then three panels show finished, held outside the nucleus, inhibitor removed.
scenes.narration: Take a cell line with no NF-κB activity, and block its protein synthesis. Lipopolysaccharide still makes the activity appear. So the protein must already have been there, inhibited. Here is the rule. Finish the activator, hold it outside the nucleus, and remove its inhibitor when the signal comes.
